Eﬀect of circulation and micro-aeration on sludge characteristics and microbial
community in an ABR for treating traditional Chinese medicine wastewater
Chengyuan Sua,b, Qiujin Denga, Yuxiang Lua, Jiaqi Pana, Wuyang Chena, Shenglong Chena, Xue Denga,
Xiangfeng Lina and Zhi Huanga
aKey Laboratory of Ecology of Rare and Endangered Species and Environmental Protection, Guangxi Normal University, Ministry of Education,
Guilin, People’s Republic of China; bUniversity Key Laboratory of Karst Ecology and Environmental Change of Guangxi Province, Guangxi Normal
University, Guilin, People’s Republic of China
ABSTRACT
The eﬀects of circulation reﬂux and micro-aeration on the performance of a modiﬁed anaerobic
baﬄed reactor (ABR) for treatment of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) wastewater were
evaluated. The characteristics of anaerobic sludge and microbial community structure in the
modiﬁed ABR were also investigated. The results indicated that with conditions of reﬂux ratio of
1, reﬂux ratio of 2, reﬂux ratio of 2 with micro-aeration, and reﬂux ratio of 3, the modiﬁed ABR
achieved an average COD removal eﬃciency of 90%, 87.7%, 87.8%, and 88.4%, respectively. In
addition, the NH3-N average removal eﬃciency was 45.1%, 50%, 55.9%, and 55.4%, respectively.
The analysis of excitation–emission matrix (EEM) ﬂuorescence spectra of soluble microbial
products (SMP) and extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) showed that there were tyrosine-
like, aromatic protein-like, and coenzyme F420 substances in the sludge. The EPS were analysed
by the Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), which showed that aromatic compounds
were partially degraded, while the protein and polysaccharide compounds increased in each
compartment of the modiﬁed ABR. Interestingly, the microbial community of anaerobic sludge
analysis results showed that Chloroﬂexi was the dominant in the ﬁrst, third and fourth
compartments. Meanwhile, Levilinea and Methanothrix were the dominant species in the ﬁrst and
third compartments at the genus level.

1. Introduction
Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is an integral part of
Chinese culture. In the medical ﬁeld, TCM has displayed
unique characteristics of eﬃcacy and curative eﬀects. In
recent years, the TCM industry has been vigorously
developed after encouragement and advocacy by the
state. However, a large amount of wastewater is pro-
duced during the production of TCM through the

process of washing, soaking, and decoction of medicinal
materials, among which the main components are poly-
saccharides, cellulose, protein and some toxic sub-
stances. People also need to address the pollution
problems caused by TCM wastewater [1]. The character-
ization of TCM wastewater is high concentrations of
organic matter, high suspended substance, complex
composition, large variation of wastewater quality, etc.
Therefore, some scholars have begun to explore the
potential treatment processes of TCM wastewater. Con-
sidering
the
characteristics
of
TCM
wastewater,
advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), membrane treat-
ment method, advanced oxidation-aerobic biological
process,
and
anaerobic-anoxic-aerobic
combined
process were employed [2–4].
In comparison to physicochemical technologies,
anaerobic processes have several advantages including
the lack of need for aeration (and thus less energy
requirement), low energy consumption, biogas pro-
duction, and withstanding of high organic-loading
[5–6]. High eﬃciency anaerobic baﬄed reactor (ABR)
processes have an important inﬂuence on the develop-
ment of modern anaerobic biological treatment tech-
nology.
ABR
has
been
extensively
used
in
the
treatment
of pulp
and
paper
mill black
liquors,
tannery, textile dye, brewery, and domestic waste-
waters
[7–10].
Researchers’
continue
to
work
to
improve and optimize ABR forms of diﬀerent types to
achieve diﬀerent treatment objectives, with the ulti-
mate goal of improving the ability of ABR’s retention
of high biomass concentrations and even distribution
of inﬂuent. These modiﬁed methods include the use
of carriers to support the growth of microorganisms,
using a larger number of compartments, and the
addition reﬂux [11]. Their results showed that reﬂux
could degrade toxic substances in wastewater, allevi-
ate inhibitory eﬀects on the ABR, and resist high
organic load of the inﬂuent. At the same time, the cir-
culation reactor signiﬁcantly improved sludge distri-
bution and mass transfer, and allowed for the direct
contact of microorganisms with the inﬂuent in each
compartment [12]. Some scholars have also studied
the eﬀects of adding micro-aeration to the ABR and
expanded granular sludge bed (EGSB) reactor [13].
Liu and Dong reported that the micro-aerobic granular
sludge reactors had stable COD removal eﬀect under
diﬀerent
operational
modes,
whereas
nitrogen
removal depended on oxygen inﬂux [13]. To our
knowledge, few scholars have combined these two
improvement methods to improve the treatment
eﬃciency; especially the eﬀects of reﬂux and micro-
aeration on the sludge characteristics and microbial
community in ABR have few investigated.
Our modiﬁed ABR was designed to increase reﬂux and
micro-aeration. The performance of a modiﬁed ABR for
treatment of TCM wastewater was investigated. In
addition, the soluble microbial products (SMP) and extra-
cellular polymeric substances (EPS) of the anaerobic
sludge was measured by excitation–emission matrix
(EEM) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy
(FTIR). Moreover, the microbial community structure in
modiﬁed ABR was explored by 16S rRNA high-through-
put sequencing.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. ABR conﬁguration
The schematic diagram of the modiﬁed ABR is shown in
Fig. S1. The ABR was made of polymethyl methacrylate.
The total volume was 12 L, and the working volume
was 10 L with length×width×height of 400 mm×100
mm×300 mm. It was divided into four compartments
included an up-ﬂow zone and a down-ﬂow zone with a
volume ratio of 3:1. The reactor was sealed and a gas
gathering system was placed in the top of each compart-
ment. The up-ﬂow zone was equipped with three
sampling ports, which was convenient for collecting
samples. The inﬂuent was fed to the reactor compart-
ments by a peristaltic pump (Longer WT600-2, Longer
pump Co., China) [10]. There was no reﬂux and micro-
aeration device at the start-up stage. After the start-up
stage, in order to improve the performance of the
reactor for treatment of real TCM wastewater, a peristal-
tic pump was added at the sampling port above the
fourth compartment to connect with the ﬁrst compart-
ment to form a reﬂux device. In addition, a micro-aera-
tion
device
was
added
in
the
fourth
reactor
compartment. The aeration process was controlled by a
gas ﬂowmeter at dissolved oxygen concentration of
0.5–1.0 mg/L.
2.2. Experimental water and inoculation sludge
In this experiment, wastewater was collected from a
TCM plant in Guilin, China. The primary characteristics
of this TCM wastewater were shown in Table 1. During
the
experiments,
the
COD
concentration
of
the
inﬂuent was controlled to approximately 2000mg/L.
NaHCO3 and nutrient solution were added in the
inﬂuent, and the pH value of the inﬂuent was kept

within values ranging 6.5–7.5. The inoculated sludge
was obtained from a brewery in Guilin city, and the
total suspended solids (TSS) of anaerobic sludge were

TSS was 0.74.
2.3. Reactors operation
This study was roughly divided into the following three
stages: sludge cultivation, sludge domestication, and
improved treatment of TCM wastewater stages. The
stage of sludge domestication culture was divided into
three phases: the ﬁrst phase was only synthetic glucose
wastewater
(A),
the
second
phase
was
synthetic
glucose wastewater and real TCM wastewater as the
composition ratio was 1:1 (B), and the third phase was
total real TCM wastewater, which each phase ran for
15–20 days and COD concentration was controlled
around 2000–2500 mg/L. The stage of improved treat-
ment was divided into four phases: reﬂux ratio of 1 (C),
reﬂux ratio of 2 (D), reﬂux ratio of 2 with micro-aeration
(E), and reﬂux ratio of 3 (F). The ABR was operated at
hydraulic residence time (HRT) 24 h and room tempera-
ture 20–25°C.
2.4. Analytical methods
During the experiment, the removal of COD and NH3-N
was analysed on each day. SMP and EPS of the sludge
in the reactor were also investigated in the diﬀerent
stages. The sludge was extracted at 45 d (stage C) and
80 d (stage E). The sludge was harvested following cen-
trifugation at 8000 rpm for 10 min; the resulting super-
natant represented the SMP [14]. The sludge pellet in
the tube was then resuspended into 15 mL of 0.05%
NaCl, sonicated at 20 KHz for 2 min, shaken horizontally
at 150 rpm for 10 min, and sonicated again for an
additional 2 min [15]. The liquor was then centrifuged
at 8000 rpm for 10 min to separate solids from the super-
natant. The collected supernatant was regarded as the
loosely bound EPS (LB-EPS). The residual sludge pellet
left in the centrifuge tube was resuspended in a 0.05%
NaCl solution, sonicated for 3 min, then heated at 80°C
for 30 min in a water bath, and ﬁnally centrifuged at
8000 rpm for 10 min to collect the tightly bound EPS
(TB-EPS) [16]. The names of the samples were ‘SMP 1-
4,’ ‘SMP R1-R4,’ ‘LB-EPS 1-4,’ ‘LB-EPS R1-R4,’ ‘TB-EPS 1-4,’
and ‘TB-EPS R1-R4,’ respectively. The analysis method
of EPS was heating extraction. Based on the identiﬁcation
of ﬂuorescent compounds, the EEM technique was
adopted to further analyse SMP and EPS components
using
a
ﬂuorescence
spectrophotometer
(F-7000,
Hitachi, Japan) [17]. In this study, the EEM ﬂuorescence
spectra were collected with subsequent scanning at
emission wavelengths from 220 to 600 nm at 5 nm
slits, and excitation wavelengths from 220 to 500 nm
also at 5 nm slits. In addition, the major functional
groups in sludge SMP and EPS were analysed by a FTIR
spectrometer (Thermo Nicolet, USA).
High-throughput sequencing was used to analyse the
microbial community variation under diﬀerent con-
ditions. The sludge samples from each compartment
were collected and mixed to a composite sample for bac-
terial DNA extraction. The qualiﬁed DNA was sequenced
through high-throughput pyrosequencing on a Miseq
sequencing platform. The polymerase chain reaction
(PCR) ampliﬁcation of the hypervariable regions used
V3-V4 universal primers 341F (CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG)
and 805R (GACTACHVGGGTATCTAATCC) for bacteria
[18,19]. The sequence was compared with the reference
microorganisms available in Ribosomal Database Project
(RDP) (http://rdp.cme.msu.edu/misc/resources.jsp), Silva
(http://www.arb-silva.de),
and
NCBI
16S
database
(http://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov). In order to obtain the species
classiﬁcation information corresponding to each oper-
ational taxonomic units (OUT), the RDP Bayesian classiﬁer
algorithm was used for taxonomic analysis of 97% simi-
larity
with
OTU
representative
sequences
[18,19].
Network analysis was performed using QIIME, and
Shannon diversity indices were calculated for each
sample. In the NCBI Sequence Read Archive database,
the biosample
accession
number
of bacteria was
SAMN10410857.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Removal eﬃciency of COD and NH3-N
TCM wastewater usually contains high organic contami-
nants. The operation stability and performance of
anaerobic reactors were usually evaluated by detecting
the removal eﬃciency of COD. The detection result of
removal COD is shown in Figure 1. At stage A, the
inﬂuent COD concentration was controlled at 2000–
2500 mg/L with a glucose substrate. At 1–15 days, the
removal eﬃciency of COD increased rapidly, and it
reached 93% on average at 15–20 days. This indicated
that anaerobic sludge has an adaptive process during
the inoculation stage, and the removal eﬃciency of
COD tends to increase over time, and could be main-
tained at more than 90%. As shown in Figure 1, after
the wastewater treatment entered into the acclimatiz-
ation stage, the COD concentration of the inﬂuent was
controlled at 1500–2300 mg/L as the glucose, real TCM
wastewater substrate, and the COD removal eﬃciency
was maintained at 93–95% in the stage B. During the
3286
C. SU ET AL.

stages C, D, E, and F, the real TCM wastewater compo-
sition became more complicated, and the COD concen-
tration in the inﬂuent was volatile when controlled
between 1000–2000mg/L. At stage C, the reﬂux device
was started. When the reﬂux ratio was 1, the removal
eﬃciency of COD was stable between 88% and 93%,
and the average removal eﬃciency of COD was 90%.
This result indicated that the sludge in the anaerobic
reactor had been successfully acclimatized from stage
B to stage C, and the treatment eﬀect was still function-
ing correctly. When the reﬂux ratio was increased to 2 at
stage D, the average removal eﬃciency of COD was
about 89%. However, at the 64th to 69th days, the
removal eﬃciency of COD reduced to 82.5%, maybe
there were complex and some bio-recalcitrant organic
compositions, phenols, humic acid, etc [1]. in the TCM
wastewater. When the reactor ran to a certain stage,
toxic substances might accumulate in the anaerobic
reactors. In addition, with reﬂux ratio increasing, some
loose sludge was washed away from the reactor, result-
ing in the SS concentration increasing in the eﬄuent
[20]. SS in the eﬄuent contributes a part of COD,
leading to the increase of COD concentration in the
eﬄuent. When the sludge adapted to the reactor, the
removal eﬃciency of COD increased back to more than
92%. At stage E, the COD removal eﬃciency remained
between 85% and 90% with the reﬂux ratio 2 and
additional
aeration.
Compared
with
stage
D,
the
removal eﬃciency of COD had a small decline. The meta-
bolic activity of methanogen in the last compartment of
the ABR was inﬂuenced by the addition of a micro aera-
tion device. Methanogens are very sensitive and need to
adapt to changing environment. At stage F, the removal
eﬃciency of COD was still maintained between 85% and
90% with reﬂux ratio 3. Through the whole process, the
removal eﬃciency of COD was always maintained
within the range of 85% to 93%, indicating that the
removal eﬃciency of COD was no signiﬁcant eﬀect by
the modiﬁed ABR with additional reﬂux ratio and micro
aeration.
In this experiment, the NH3-N removal eﬃciency was
also discussed (Figure 1). Because of the composition
of TCM wastewater, the NH3-N concentration could not
be controlled stably. At stage B, glucose and real TCM
wastewater constituted the majority of the inﬂuent.
The NH3-N removal eﬃciency was about 53%. The
removal eﬃciency of NH3-N in stage C was between
40% and 50%, and the average removal eﬃciency of
NH3-N was 45%, which indicated that the removal
eﬃciency of NH3-N did not increase obvious at the
reﬂux ratio of 1. Compared with only real TCM waste-
water, the composition of glucose provides a biodegrad-
able carbon source which is why the removal eﬃciency
of NH3-N was higher. In stage D with a reﬂux ratio of 2,
the average removal eﬃciency of NH3-N reached to
50%. After increasing micro-aeration in stage E, the
average removal eﬃciency of NH3-N increased to 56%,
and the removal eﬃciency was between 53% and 65%.
The NH3-N concentration was kept between 12–20 mg/
L in the eﬄuent during this time. Increasing the
amount of dissolved oxygen in the inﬂuent after micro-
aeration allows the ammonia nitrogen to convert to
nitrite nitrogen by nitrifying bacteria under aerobic
environment of the modiﬁed ABR. Nitriﬁcation process
was present in the reactor [21]. In stage F, the NH3-N
removal eﬃciency ranged from 49% to 66%. Here, it
was illustrated that the increasing reﬂux ratio and
micro-aeration was beneﬁted the removal eﬃciency of
NH3-N.
3.2. Sludge characteristics
Before and after the improvement, changes in the sludge
characteristics were analysed in the modiﬁed ABR. Pre-
vious studies have reported considerable variability in
the production of SMP in response to environmental
stresses imposed by the microorganisms [14,15]. From

another perspective, the ingredients and proportions of
proteins, polysaccharides, and other polymers in the
EPS of anaerobic sludge were closely related to the
microbial communities and their living environment.
Additionally, the sludge sedimentation performance,
physicochemical
character,
surface
features
of
the
sludge, and biological ﬂocculation properties, were
inﬂuenced by EPS [22–25]. Therefore, the SMP and EPS
in each compartment of the reactor were analysed by
EEM and FTIR spectra.
3.2.1. EEM ﬂuorescence spectra analysis
EEM spectroscopy is an important technique for monitor-
ing and analysing bioreactors. It has the characteristics of
high sensitivity, requiring fewer samples, high accuracy,
and good speed. As shown in Figure 2, before the
Figure 2. EEM ﬂuorescence spectra of SMP in each compartment.

modiﬁcation, the SMP of sludge in the reactor had three
ﬂuorescence peaks in the EEM spectra, which were of a
type of tyrosine-like ﬂuorescence peak (Ex/Em = 280/
310 nm), fulvic acid-like ﬂuorescence peak (Ex/Em =
325/350 nm), and humic acid-like ﬂuorescence peak
(Ex/Em = 340/410 nm). After improvement of reﬂux and
micro-aeration, the SMP of the sludge mainly had four
ﬂuorescence peaks; tyrosine-like ﬂuorescence peak (Ex/
Em = 280/310 nm), humic acid-like ﬂuorescence peak
(Ex/Em = 340/410 nm), fulvic acid-like ﬂuorescence peak
(Ex/Em = 325/350 nm), and another class fulvic acid-like
ﬂuorescence peak (Ex/Em = 260/420 nm) in the EEM
spectra of each compartment [20,26]. For the ﬁrst com-
partment, the absorption peak intensity of tyrosine-like
increased slightly, while the absorption peak intensity
of humic acid-like decreased. The contents of humic
acid-like were reduced in the ﬁrst compartment to
avoid
acidiﬁcation,
and
the
contents
of
tyrosine
increased in the ﬁrst compartment of anaerobic sludge
to promote the physiological activities of microorgan-
isms in the reactor. The intensity of tyrosine-like and
humic acid-like ﬂuorescence absorption peaks decreased
at a small range in the EEM spectra of the sludge in the
second reactor compartment, which showed that after
the modiﬁcation, the contents of SMP decreased in the
second compartment of the reactor. It was illustrated
that the microbes consumed more protein to supply
their own metabolism and the microbial activity was
more active in the second compartment. The content
of humic acid-like reduction could avoid acidiﬁcation in
the reactor with additional reﬂux ratio and micro aera-
tion which made the reactor operate stably. The intensity
of humic acid-like absorption peak in the EEM spectra of
SMP reduced in the third compartment of the modiﬁed
ABR. This result showed that the improvement reﬂux
ratio could also reduce toxic substances in the third
reactor compartment of the reactor. In EEM spectra of
SMP, the absorption peak of tyrosine-like signiﬁcantly
increased, while the absorption peak of humic acid-like
decreased in the fourth compartment of the modiﬁed
ABR. The results showed that TCM wastewater was eﬀec-
tively treated in the fourth reactor compartment after the
improvement reﬂux ratio. In conclusion, it was demon-
strated that the visible fulvic acid-like absorption peak
appeared, and visible humic acid-like absorption peak
decreased, avoiding the acidiﬁcation of the reactor in
each compartment after the modiﬁcation. This was con-
sistent with the high removal rate of COD and NH3-N in
the modiﬁed ABR.
This was all except for the second compartment,
where the content of tyrosine increased in each compart-
ment of the reactor. Previous studies have shown that
the formation of anaerobic granular sludge has a close
relationship with tyrosine. Therefore, the contaminants
in the TCM wastewater were eﬀectively degraded and
the modiﬁed ABR was stably operated. In Figure 3,
before modiﬁcation of reﬂux and micro-aeration, the
LB-EPS mainly had ﬁve ﬂuorescence peaks in the EEM
spectra of each compartment, which was characterized
by tyrosine-like (Ex/Em = 290/345 nm), fulvic acid-like
(Ex/Em = 325/350 nm), coenzyme NADH (Ex/Em = 335/
420 nm), another class fulvic acid-like (Ex/Em = 390/
430 nm), and coenzyme F420 ﬂuorescence peaks (Ex/
Em = 420/475 nm) [20,21]. After modiﬁcation, the inten-
sity of the coenzyme F420 ﬂuorescence absorption peak
was signiﬁcantly reduced, the intensity of the coenzyme
NADH ﬂuorescence absorption peak increased, and the
intensity of the protein absorption peak increased
slightly in amplitude during the ﬁrst compartment of
the reactor. It was shown in the treatment that methano-
gens decayed in the ﬁrst compartment because of micro-
aeration. The ﬂuorescence intensity of fulvic acid-like and
coenzyme
F420
increased
slightly,
indicating
that
methane-producing activity was present in the second
compartment. At the same time, the intensity of coen-
zyme NADH ﬂuorescence absorption peak was signiﬁ-
cantly increased. The ﬂuorescence intensity of protein-
like also tended to increase. The increasing ﬂuorescence
intensity of coenzyme F420 indicated that the second
compartment was in good operating condition. In the
third compartment, the ﬂuorescence peak of humic
acid-like (Ex/Em = 300/470 nm) appeared. However, the
humic acid disappeared after improvement. At the
same time, the ﬂuorescence intensity of protein and
coenzyme NADH increased. In addition, the ﬂuorescence
intensity of coenzyme F420, coenzyme NADH, ﬂuvic acid-
like, and protein-like increased signiﬁcantly in the fourth
compartment, especially those of coenzyme F420 and
protein-like. The reason may be that in the fourth com-
partment of the reactor, addition of the aeration device
created an environment where the strictly anaerobic
microorganisms could not adapt to the environment
and then declined in number, while the facultative anae-
robe would enter a hypermetabolic state. On a whole,
the microbial metabolism was vigorous in the fourth
compartment after the modiﬁcation. The toxic sub-
stances in TCM wastewater were degraded, which was
conducive to the stable operation of the reactor. In
other words, it was demonstrated that after the modiﬁ-
cation of reﬂux and micro-aeration, there was an increas-
ing trend in the amount of protein-like substances and
coenzyme NADH in each compartment. Therefore, the
stability of sludge could be improved, which provided
a guarantee for the operation of the modiﬁed ABR.
As shown in Fig. S2, the three main ﬂuorescence

were

3.2.2. FTIR spectra analysis
FTIR spectroscopy has the advantages of high scanning
speed, good reproducibility, and high signal-to-noise
ratio. It is usually used to analyse the functional groups
and molecular structures in SMP and EPS in order to
determine the content of aromatic compounds, proteins,
polysaccharides, and other substances contained in

4. Conclusions
The results showed that the modiﬁcation to add reﬂux
and micro-aeration devices in the ABR had a signiﬁcant
impact on the removal eﬃciency of NH3-N and the
microbial community. The protein-like substances of
sludge in each compartment increased, while the
humic acid and aromatic compounds decreased in
each compartment of the modiﬁed ABR. After the
improvement, the relative abundance of Planctomyce-
tales and Syntrophobacterales increased, while Methano-
thrix was negatively aﬀected in the reactor. This research
will be helpful for the operation and useful for improving
the performance of ABR.
